facts.text: Star Crispin Glover came up with the idea for his magician Montag the Magnificent to wear a codpiece. Crew on set described its "gigantic" size to Dread Central.
Crispin Glover told JoBlo he "didn't sign the contract until it was written": the remake dropped scenes he loved from the 1970 original, so he insisted they be put back in.
The whole shoot took just 22 days. Director Jeremy Kasten's crew filled a dilapidated Los Angeles with extras, bands and practical makeup effects.
The 1970 original was directed by splatter pioneer Herschell Gordon Lewis on an estimated $60,000 budget, shot in about two weeks. Its gore reportedly used sheep carcasses.
Jeffrey Combs was the first actor cast, and his role, The Geek, was written specifically for him. He spent three hours in the makeup chair.
Jeffrey Combs' Geek eats maggots and a cockroach and bites the head off a rat. Director Jeremy Kasten said Combs, in ragged beard and makeup, sometimes startled people on set.
Director Jeremy Kasten said Crispin Glover's Montag went "in kind of a Siegfried & Roy direction": flamboyant and over the top.
Suicide Girl Amina was the first of the Suicide Girls cast. She really is missing a leg below the knee, so that was worked into her stage act with Montag.
The Suicide Girls' fake bodies and prosthetics had to be matched to the women's real tattoos, with mostly practical effects, according to director Jeremy Kasten.
Director Jeremy Kasten called the film a "love letter" to downtown Los Angeles. Most of it was shot at the Park Plaza Hotel there.
Writer Zach Chassler described the remake as "splatter-noir." Director Jeremy Kasten said he aimed for a garish, giallo-inspired Italian horror look.
Kip Pardue (Edmund Bigelow) said this was his first horror movie. He also played football at Yale and modeled for Armani and Polo.
Kasten's carnival scenes were shot at an abandoned motel turned performance-art haunted house, the "Circus of Horrors," with 100+ extras and the band The Death Riders playing.
The blood wrestling at the carnival was improvised at the last minute.
Rock band The Who's singer Roger Daltrey was once interested in acting in this movie, but his girlfriend disapproved of the script.
Crispin Glover insisted the "final illusion speech" from the original 1970 film be shot for the remake. It was filmed but ended up only in the deleted scenes.
Crispin Glover told JoBlo the 1970 original has ties to Videodrome: "there are certainly reality plays within that original film," with people hypnotized through television.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave the remake 2 stars out of 5, saying the digital gore "looks like fakery" next to Herschell Gordon Lewis' original, though he credited Crispin Glover's over-the-top turn.
In the 1970 original, the first actor cast as Montag left the set after a clash, and crew member Ray Sager took the lead instead.
The film was first planned to be shot in 3D.
Brad Dourif plays Dr. Chong, a role first written as Asian. Director Jeremy Kasten called Dourif "unnerving to the core."
Brad Dourif is the voice of Chucky in all seven Child's Play films, and he earned an Oscar nomination for his debut in One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.
Co-star Bijou Phillips (Maggie) went on to Hostel: Part II. Kip Pardue, who plays Edmund Bigelow, later starred in Hostel: Part III.
Bijou Phillips was the youngest model ever on a Vogue cover, on the Italian edition, shortly after appearing on Interview magazine's cover at age 13.
Crispin Glover played George McFly in Back to the Future. After a pay dispute he skipped the sequels, which is why Part II centers on his character being killed.
Jeffrey Combs starred in Re-Animator as Herbert West and played Weyoun and Shran in Star Trek. He's been called "the first Lovecraftian actor" by H.P. Lovecraft fans.
Flux Suicide wore panties for the shots of her on stage nude in front of a live audience.
The plot's explanation for audience suggestibility is a drug called Tetrodetosone. Moria's Richard Scheib said that drug-based explanation weakens the original's strangeness.
Makeup effects were designed by Keith Christensen, Jason Collins and Elvis Jones. Steve Porcaro composed the score.
Director Jeremy Kasten doubled Kip Pardue's hands for several insert shots.
Director Jeremy Kasten said he was once a Suicide Girls member himself and wanted to bring that world into the film.
Writer Zach Chassler also wrote a treatment for She-Devils, a larger-budget remake of another Herschell Gordon Lewis film, according to Dread Central's set visit.
The film premiered June 22, 2007 at the LA Film Festival, then opened at the Landmark Theater on June 28. DVD followed August 19, 2008.
Dread Central's Steve Barton gave the film 4 out of 5, writing "I applaud it for its overall insanity." Bloody Disgusting said it made the original worse.
Director Jeremy Kasten also made The Thirst, All Soul's Day, and a segment of the anthology The Theatre Bizarre.
Crispin Glover has toured his own art films, like What Is It?, for years without a normal theatrical release, appearing live at each screening.
The 2007 remake appears in the documentary American Grindhouse (2010). The 1970 original's footage also shows up in the 2007 film Juno.
The closing credits roll sideways, from the right of the screen to the left.
Production companies Open Sky Entertainment and Sick-o-Scope Motion Pictures made the film. Christopher Duddy was both producer and cinematographer.
